title: Infusions and Transfusions
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Infusions and Transfusions in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Intravenous infusions and blood transfusions are fundamental clinical skills that nursing students in Nigeria must master to ensure patient safety and effective healthcare delivery. An infusion involves the administration of fluids, medications, or nutrients directly into a patient's venous system, primarily to maintain fluid and electrolyte balance, correct hypovolemia, or deliver pharmacologic agents. On the other hand, a blood transfusion specifically refers to the intravenous administration of whole blood or specific blood components, such as packed red blood cells, platelets, or fresh frozen plasma, to restore oxygen-carrying capacity, clotting factors, or volume following acute blood loss, trauma, or during surgeries. Nurses play a vital and independent role in managing these therapies. From assessing the patient's baseline clinical status and verifying physicians' orders to calculating drop rates and monitoring for adverse reactions, nursing responsibilities require vigilance, critical thinking, and strict adherence to hospital policies. In resource-constrained settings like Nigeria, where obstetric hemorrhage, severe malaria-induced anemia, and traumatic injuries are prevalent, timely and safe administration of intravenous fluids and blood products can be life-saving. Therefore, understanding the pharmacological properties of infusion fluids, the immunological considerations of blood groups, and the physiological responses of the human body is essential for every nursing professional. Proper training helps prevent complications like fluid overload, air embolism, and acute hemolytic transfusion reactions, thereby promoting optimal patient recovery and reducing morbidity and mortality rates across healthcare institutions.

headings.title: Types of Intravenous Infusions and Blood Products
headings.content: Intravenous infusions and blood products are categorized based on their clinical utility and composition. Intravenous infusions generally fall into crystalloid and colloid categories. Crystalloids, such as Normal Saline (0.9% Sodium Chloride) and Ringer's Lactate, are aqueous solutions of mineral salts or other water-soluble molecules that easily flow across the capillary membrane, making them ideal for initial resuscitation and maintenance fluid therapy. Colloids, such as human albumin or dextrans, contain larger insoluble molecules that remain in the intravascular space, increasing oncotic pressure to pull fluid into the circulation. Blood products, managed by blood banks and clinical teams, include several vital components tailored to specific patient deficits. Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs) are utilized to increase hemoglobin and hematocrit levels in patients with symptomatic anemia or acute blood loss without expanding total blood volume excessively. Platelets are administered to patients with thrombocytopenia or active bleeding disorders to assist in blood clotting. Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) provides essential coagulation factors for individuals experiencing clotting factor deficiencies or massive transfusions. Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen and factor VIII, primarily used for hemophilia and von Willebrand disease. Whole blood, though less commonly used today due to component therapy efficiency, contains all blood elements and is indicated for massive acute hemorrhage. Understanding these specific types allows nurses to anticipate physician orders and tailor patient monitoring strategies to the specific fluid or blood product being infused.

headings.title: Composition of Crystalloids, Colloids, and Blood Components
headings.content: A thorough understanding of the composition of crystalloids, colloids, and blood components is critical for safe fluid management in nursing practice. Crystalloids are categorized into isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic solutions. Isotonic solutions, like 0.9% Normal Saline and Hartmann's solution (Ringer's Lactate), have an effective osmolality close to extracellular fluid, causing no fluid shift between compartments. Hypotonic solutions, such as 0.45% Normal Saline, have a lower osmolality, causing water to move from the intravascular space into the intracellular and interstitial compartments, which is useful in treating cellular dehydration. Hypertonic solutions, like 3% Sodium Chloride, have a higher osmolality, pulling water out of cells into the extracellular space, indicated for severe hyponatremia. Colloids like human albumin, gelatin solutions, and starches act as volume expanders due to their high molecular weight. Blood components are complex biological tissues requiring precise physiological composition matching. Whole blood consists of red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, and plasma suspended in an anticoagulant preservative solution. PRBCs are derived by removing most of the plasma from whole blood, reducing volume overload risks. Platelets are suspended in a small volume of plasma and must be stored at room temperature with agitation, unlike PRBCs which require refrigeration. FFP contains all coagulation factors and must be thawed before administration. Knowing the exact composition helps nurses anticipate physiological responses, such as electrolyte shifts, shifts in fluid compartments, and potential immune reactions.

headings.title: Preparation and Safety Protocols for Infusions and Transfusions
headings.content: Preparation and safety protocols form the bedrock of safe infusion and transfusion therapy. Before initiating any intravenous infusion or blood transfusion, nurses must execute rigorous checks to prevent medication errors and catastrophic transfusion reactions. For standard intravenous fluids, the nurse must verify the physician's order against the patient's chart, inspect the fluid bag for clarity, expiration date, and integrity, and ensure the correct flow rate is calculated. For blood transfusions, safety protocols are even more stringent due to the risks of immunological mismatch. Two qualified healthcare professionals must independently perform a bedside blood-product verification. This involves checking the patient's identification band against the blood bag label, blood bank compatibility form, and hospital ID number, verifying the ABO and Rh groups, checking the unit number, and confirming the expiration date. Blood products must be inspected for abnormal discoloration, clots, or hemolysis. Furthermore, blood must be retrieved from the blood bank only when the patient's intravenous access is secured and running with 0.9% Normal Saline, as other solutions like Ringer's Lactate can cause calcium-induced clotting. Standard blood administration sets equipped with a built-in filter must always be used to trap microaggregates. Pre-medications, such as antihistamines or antipyretics, may be ordered for patients with a history of minor transfusion reactions. Maintaining strict aseptic technique during cannula insertion and line connection prevents hospital-acquired bloodstream infections, completing a comprehensive safety framework.

headings.title: Administration Techniques and Patient Monitoring
headings.content: Administration techniques and vigilant patient monitoring are paramount duties for the nursing student and professional. The procedure begins with explaining the process to the patient and obtaining informed consent for blood products. The nurse selects an appropriate peripheral vein, typically in the forearm or hand, using an intravenous cannula of adequate gauge (e.g., 18G or 20G for blood to prevent hemolysis). Once access is established and flushed, the infusion or transfusion is initiated at the prescribed rate. For blood transfusions, specific protocols dictate that the infusion must start slowly—usually no more than 2 milliliters per minute or about 50 mL for the first 15 minutes—while the nurse remains at the bedside. This initial window is critical because most acute hemolytic or severe allergic reactions occur within the first 50 mL of blood infusion. Vital signs (temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation) must be recorded immediately before starting, 15 minutes after initiation, every 30 minutes to an hour during the procedure, and upon completion. The nurse must monitor for signs of circulatory overload, such as dyspnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, and crackles in the lungs, particularly in vulnerable populations like pediatric, elderly, or cardiac patients. Blood products must be infused within a maximum timeframe of four hours to prevent bacterial proliferation at room temperature. Accurate intake and output charting must be maintained throughout the duration of therapy to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention and prevent fluid imbalance.

headings.title: Complications and Emergency Management of Transfusion Reactions
headings.content: Despite rigorous safety protocols, complications can arise during infusions and transfusions, requiring prompt recognition and emergency management by nurses. Infusion-related complications include infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, air embolism, and circulatory fluid overload. If phlebitis or infiltration occurs, the nurse must immediately stop the infusion, remove the cannula, apply appropriate compresses, and select a new site. Blood transfusion reactions are particularly dangerous and are classified as acute or delayed, immunological or non-immunological. Acute hemolytic reactions, caused by ABO incompatibility, present with fever, chills, chest pain, lower back pain, tachycardia, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria. Allergic reactions range from mild urticaria to severe anaphylaxis with bronchospasm and shock. Febrile non-hemolytic reactions involve fever and chills without hemolysis, often due to donor leukocyte antibodies. Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO) and Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI) are severe respiratory complications characterized by severe dyspnea and hypoxia, though TRALI presents with non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema and normal central venous pressure, whereas TACO presents with volume overload signs. In the event of any suspected transfusion reaction, the nurse must act instantly: 1) Stop the transfusion immediately; 2) Disconnect the blood tubing and replace it with a fresh set running 0.9% Normal Saline to keep the vein open; 3) Notify the physician and blood bank immediately; 4) Monitor vital signs closely; 5) Return the blood bag, tubing, and post-reaction blood and urine samples to the blood bank; and 6) Document the event thoroughly and complete an incident report.
